Need to search first.I could only check part of this passage properly. My search tool hit its usage limit early, so I couldn't open any page in full. Every note below comes from the search-result extracts I did get. That means there's nothing for some verses (123–125, 128, 132–134, 136, 145–147), and where you asked for traditions and other views, there's less than you wanted. I'd suggest running a second pass on the Pe (129–136) and Qoph (145–152) sections.

**Notes on the sources.** The commentators cited come from these backgrounds:
- **Reformed:** Calvin, the Geneva Bible notes.
- **Baptist:** Spurgeon, Gill.
- **Methodist:** Adam Clarke, Benson.
- **Nonconformist / Presbyterian:** Matthew Henry, Poole.
- **Calvary Chapel:** Chuck Smith.

Luther and the Greek and Latin translations (Septuagint and Vulgate) only appear second-hand, as other writers quote them. None of the pages I saw describe a real split between denominations on these verses. The differences I found are between individual commentators, and I've marked them where they come up.

---

**v. 118**
- Keil & Delitzsch say "their deceit is in vain" doesn't mean their scheming fails. It means their deceiving of themselves and others is falsehood with no truth holding it together. They also reject a variant reading found in the Greek and Syriac. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-120.htm
- Constable takes vv. 118–119 together: God will judge those who look down on His word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-120.html

**v. 119**
- Coffman reads the image of the wicked thrown away like dross as a glimpse of the final judgment. He sees the psalmist's trembling in v. 120 as confirming this. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-120.html
- Calvin links "dross" to v. 120. Watching God reject the wicked filled the psalmist with horror, and that brought him to fear God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-120.html
- Clarke (Methodist) says the wicked are worthless in God's sight. One reason the psalmist loves God's testimonies is to escape the judgments that fall on the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/csb/psalms/119-120.html
- Keil & Delitzsch discuss an alternative reading, "I reckon them as dross," found in some ancient Greek versions and Jerome. They reject it as too narrow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-120.htm

**v. 120**
- On the Hebrew word: Ellicott, Calvin, Gill and the Cambridge Bible say "trembles" is literally the hair standing on end in terror (compare Job 4:15).
  - https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-120.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-120.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) says even the psalmist's "flesh" dreaded offending so great a God. Love in v. 119 fits with fear in v. 120: tormenting fear is driven out, but the reverent fear of a child towards a father remains. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_113-120.cfm
- Matthew Henry says that instead of gloating over those under God's displeasure, the psalmist humbled himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-120.html
- Barnes calls reverent awe an essential part of all true religion. The Cambridge Bible quotes Archbishop Leighton: the flesh is awed by God's judgments, while the soul is bound to Him by love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-120.htm
- **Where commentators differ: whose judgment is he afraid of?**
  - Gill (Baptist) says it is not fear of God's wrath or damnation falling on himself. It is fear of what is coming on the wicked. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-120.html
  - Poole says the psalmist also feared for himself. He knew his own sins and feared God might punish him too, or that he might join in their sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-120.htm
  - Clarke (Methodist) says he was often alarmed in case he fell short. Only assurance of God's mercy can save him from distressing fears. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-120.html
  - The Geneva notes (Reformed) say the fear came from his own weakness, and that this fear leads to repentance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-120.htm
- **Other view (ancient versions):** Brenton's translation of the Greek Old Testament reads "Penetrate my flesh with thy fear." https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-120.htm

**v. 121–122**
- I only found one note. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain v. 122 (KJV "be surety") as "stand for me against my oppressors," comparing Gen 43:9 and Isa 38:14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-126.htm
- Gene Getz sums up vv. 121–128 this way: love God's word and will more than any earthly possession. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalms-principles-gene-getz

**v. 126**
- **Two possible readings.** Barnes notes the Hebrew literally says "time to do for Yahweh." It can mean "time for the LORD to act" or "time for us to act for the LORD." Barnes prefers the first, because the verse speaks to God directly. He still finds the second meaningful: God's people should stir themselves when the law is despised. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-126.html
  - The Cambridge Bible also prefers "time for the LORD to act" in judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-126.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch go the other way and prefer "time to act for the LORD." They say the idea of God stepping in to judge doesn't fit the context. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-126.htm
  - Gill reports that the Greek Septuagint and the Aramaic Targum take it as "time to work for the Lord" or "do the will of the Lord." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-126.html
  - Matthew Henry says the original allows both. On the second reading, everyone should take the Lord's side as ungodliness grows. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-126.html
- Calvin (Reformed) says God may seem to take no notice for a time, but He delays His judgments for wise reasons and carries them out when the time is right. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-126.html
- Spurgeon: David was a servant, so it was always his time to work. But seeing human wickedness, he felt his Master's hand was needed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_121-128.cfm
- Gill also reads the verse as about Christ: a call for God to send the Messiah to fulfil the broken law and uphold its honour. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-126.html
- The Geneva notes: when the wicked have brought everything to confusion, that is God's time to help. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-126.htm
- Clarke reads it historically, with the Babylonians as "they." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-126.html
- Chuck Smith applies it to his own nation and says God will act "very shortly." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-126.html
- **Other views:** A Bible Hub article says Jewish writers between the Testaments applied the verse to the Maccabean crisis (1 Macc 2:44–45). It also says the Talmud (Berakhot 63a) used it to justify protecting the Torah when society ignored it. I'm only reporting the article; I didn't check those sources. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Psalm_119_126_LORD_act.htm

**v. 127**
- Ellicott: the godlessness of the wicked makes the Law even more precious to the psalmist. What they reject, he treasures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-126.htm
- MacLaren: seeing others turn away makes the psalmist grip the law more tightly, and their contempt makes him love it more. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-126.htm
- A sermon on the same page (Henry Melvill) offers another link: because God is about to judge, the righteous feel the worth of His commandments most in times of danger. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-126.htm

**v. 129**
- Keil & Delitzsch: "wonderful" means paradoxical things, above everyday life and ordinary understanding. Here "keep" means careful, prolonged study until he understands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-130.htm
- S. Conway (sermon) thinks the brighter tone of this section shows help had come to the psalmist through God's word. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-130.htm

**v. 130**
- On the word "unfolding": Barnes, JFB, Ellicott and Keil & Delitzsch take the Hebrew to mean "opening," "unfolding" or "explaining" God's word, rather than the word entering the mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-130.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch add that God Himself opens up His word to those eager to learn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-130.htm
- Calvin: the truth revealed in God's word is so clear that the very first sight of it enlightens the mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-130.html
- Clarke: when I open my Bible, light springs up. Every sermon and prayer is an opening that lets light in. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-130.html
- Matthew Henry:
  - Scripture is the ordinary means the Spirit uses to give light.
  - Even its first verses enlighten.
  - Explaining the word is most useful when ministers "give the sense" (Neh 8:8).
  - Some apply the verse to the New Testament unfolding the Old.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-130.html
- Gill: the word lightens a person once the Lord opens the heart by His Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-130.htm
- "The simple": Barnes says the word means those easily persuaded or inexperienced. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-130.htm
- **Traditions and ancient versions:** Barnes reports that the Greek and Latin translations read "declaration" or "manifestation." He gives Luther's translation as: when God's word is revealed, it delivers and makes the simple wise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-130.htm

**v. 131**
- Matthew Henry: when the psalmist was kept away from public worship he longed for it again, and when he had it he drank in the word like a newborn baby. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61170/
- William Cowper (quoted on the same page) cites church fathers on the image:
  - Basil: it shows the soul leaning towards God's word.
  - Ambrose: the open mouth is the mouth of the inner person, the heart.
  - Euthymius: it shows intense longing.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61170/
- Henry Melvill gives two readings: one intense longing, or two separate clauses, the first expressing deep dissatisfaction. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/61170/

**v. 135**
- A sermon notes that the Hebrew word translated "gives light" in v. 130 is also used of God's shining face here. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-130.htm
- Getz sums up vv. 129–136: show compassion to those who ignore God's word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalms-principles-gene-getz

**v. 137–138**
- Coffman: this section stresses God's righteousness and extends it to His word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-139.html
- Matthew Henry: God never has done, and never can do, wrong. His promises are kept. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch on v. 138: "in righteousness and faithfulness" describes how God gave His law, out of His holiness and His honest desire for people's good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm

**v. 139**
- Spurgeon: zeal like a fire in the soul. People's forgetting of God fanned it until it nearly consumed him. Their contempt filled him with holy anger. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps119_137-144.cfm
- Calvin: what grieved him was not his own wrongs but the breaking of God's law. We are easily angered when we are hurt, yet unmoved by offences against God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-139.html
- Barnes makes the same point: worry if all your feelings are about wrongs done to you and none about God being dishonoured. Barnes also notes the margin reading "cut me off." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm
- Gill (Baptist): a burning love that wore down his body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-139.html
- Matthew Henry: zeal should push us to do what we can against sin, or at least to be better ourselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-139.html
- Poole: "forgotten" means despising and disobeying. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm
- **Reading it about Christ:** Bishop Horne, quoted by Benson (Methodist), says only the Son of God could say this with complete truth. He points to John 2:17 and Psalm 69:9. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm

**v. 140**
- Keil & Delitzsch: God's word is pure, fire-tested, the finest metal (Ps 12:6; 18:30). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm
- Matthew Henry: loving God's word is evidence of loving God, because the word is meant to make us share His holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm

**v. 141**
- Keil & Delitzsch report that the Greek and Latin versions read "young" instead of "small" or "lowly." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm
- Matthew Henry: when we are small and despised, we need God's precepts all the more to hold us up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm

**v. 142**
- Matthew Henry: God's law is the truth and the standard of holiness, but only Christ's obedience justifies the believer. This is a Reformation distinction: the law shows what is right, but it doesn't save. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm

**v. 143–144**
- Matthew Henry:
  - Saints often enjoy the delights of God's word most when they are in trouble.
  - On "that I may live" he quotes John 17:3: eternal life is knowing God and Christ.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-139.htm
- Bridgeway: in vv. 141–144 the psalmist finds God's word reliable and a constant comfort. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-139.html

**v. 145–147**
- I only found summaries of the whole section. Getz says to pray earnestly in a crisis, using God's word as the basis. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalms-principles-gene-getz
- Guzik's title for vv. 145–152 is "Praying to the God of the Bible." https://enduringword.com/sermons/psalms/psalms/
